formation.title: The Land of a Million Elephants
formation.text:
The Lao lands are reunited under a single crown. From the misty highlands of Muang Sua to the broad plains of the Khorat Plateau, the ancient principalities have recognized a common sovereign. The Mekong River, which has always been the lifeline of the Lao people, now flows through a single kingdom.

Fa Ngum founded this realm with the blessing of Khmer arms and Buddhist dharma, naming it Lan Xang Hom Khao: the Land of a Million Elephants and the White Parasol. The elephants represent the military might that forged the kingdom; the parasol represents the Buddhist faith that gives it meaning.

Which legacy shall define our restored kingdom?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Let the earth tremble beneath our elephants!

modifiers.name: The Million Elephants
modifiers.text: The war elephants of Lan Xang are more than beasts of burden. They are the living embodiment of royal power, each one a fortress of flesh and ivory that turns the tide of battle. The kingdom that commands a million elephants commands the fear of all who oppose it.

options.text: Let the dharma illuminate our path.

modifiers.name: The White Parasol
modifiers.text: Under the white parasol of dharma, the kingdom finds its truest strength, not in the clash of arms, but in the wisdom of the sangha, the beauty of the wat, and the harmony of a people united by faith. The parasol shelters all who seek its shade.

advances.name: Elephant Warfare
advances.text: The war elephant tradition that gives Lan Xang its very name: the Land of a Million Elephants.

advances.name: Theravada Sangha
advances.text: The Buddhist monastic order that forms the spiritual and educational foundation of Lao society.

advances.name: Sticky Rice Tradition
advances.text: The cultivation of glutinous rice, the staple food that defines Lao cuisine and communal life.

advances.name: Fa Ngum's Legacy
advances.text: The military traditions established by Fa Ngum during his conquest and unification of the Lao principalities in 1353.

advances.name: Khmer Heritage
advances.text: The cultural and diplomatic ties to the Khmer court, where Fa Ngum grew up in exile and from which he drew the Buddhist traditions that shaped Lan Xang.

advances.name: Silk Weaving Tradition
advances.text: The art of Lao silk weaving, passed down through generations and producing textiles prized across Southeast Asia.

advances.name: Mekong River Trade
advances.text: The development of trade networks along the Mekong River, the economic artery of Lan Xang.

advances.name: River Fleet
advances.text: Patrol craft designed for the Mekong and its tributaries, securing trade routes and projecting power along the waterways.

advances.name: Forest Product Trade
advances.text: The export of valuable forest products (benzoin resin, lac, and hardwoods) from the dense forests of the Lao highlands.

advances.name: Samsenthai's Reforms
advances.text: The trade and administrative reforms of King Samsenthai, Fa Ngum's son, who transformed Lan Xang from a conquest state into a prosperous trading kingdom.

advances.name: The Phra Bang Palladium
advances.text: The sacred Buddha image that serves as the palladium of the Lao kingdom, a symbol of divine favor and royal legitimacy.

event.title: The Arrival of the Phra Bang
event.text:
A sacred Buddha image has come to our kingdom: the Phra Bang, said to have been cast in Sri Lanka and carried through the courts of the Khmer before finding its home among the Lao people. Fashioned from an alloy of gold, silver, and bronze, the Phra Bang stands in the gesture of dispelling fear, its palms turned outward in blessing.

King Visounarath has declared it the palladium of the realm. Where the Phra Bang resides, there is the spiritual heart of Lan Xang. The city of Luang Prabang itself takes its name from this sacred image, Luang meaning 'great' and Prabang for the Buddha it shelters.

Monks and pilgrims have already begun to journey from across the kingdom to pay homage. The Phra Bang is more than a religious artifact; it is a symbol that the dharma has chosen Lan Xang as its home.

options.text: May the Phra Bang bless our kingdom forever.

advances.name: Elephant Corps
advances.text: The formalized elephant warfare corps that made Lan Xang's armies feared throughout mainland Southeast Asia.

advances.name: Pha That Luang
advances.text: The great golden stupa of Vientiane, the most sacred monument in the Lao kingdom and a beacon of Theravada Buddhism.

advances.name: Ivory Craft
advances.text: The tradition of ivory carving, drawing on Lan Xang's vast elephant herds to produce luxury goods for export.

advances.name: Vientiane as Capital
advances.text: The establishment of Vientiane as the permanent capital of Lan Xang by King Setthathirath, chosen for its strategic position on the Mekong.

advances.name: Resistance Against Burma
advances.text: The guerrilla tactics and strategic retreats that allowed Lan Xang to survive against the vastly larger Burmese Empire.

event.title: The Resistance of Setthathirath
event.text:
King Bayinnaung of Burma has hurled his vast armies against Lan Xang, but our king has proven equal to the challenge. Setthathirath moved the capital from venerable Luang Prabang to strategic Vientiane, where the broad Mekong provides a natural moat. When the Burmese came, he refused open battle with their superior numbers and instead waged a war of jungle ambush and scorched earth.

In 1570, after Bayinnaung's retreat, Setthathirath counterattacked, capturing more than 30,000 prisoners and 100 war elephants from the fleeing Burmese columns. But the king is also a builder: Wat Xieng Thong in Luang Prabang and the great Pha That Luang stupa in Vientiane stand as testaments to his dual nature.

Shall we honor Setthathirath as warrior or as builder?

options.text: The jungle is our fortress. Let none pass!

modifiers.name: Defender of the Realm
modifiers.text: Like Setthathirath before the Burmese host, the kingdom stands resolute. Every mountain pass becomes a deathtrap, every jungle trail a snare for the invader.

options.text: Our temples shall outlast any army.

modifiers.name: The Temple Builder
modifiers.text: In the tradition of Setthathirath, who raised Wat Xieng Thong and Pha That Luang, the kingdom channels its energy into monuments that will outlast any conqueror.

advances.name: River Warfare
advances.text: Specialized infantry trained in jungle and river combat, protecting the Mekong trade routes from raiders and invaders.

advances.name: Lacquerware Industry
advances.text: The production of fine lacquerware from forest-harvested lac resin, a valued luxury craft of the Lao artisan tradition.

advances.name: Haw Kham Palace
advances.text: The royal palace tradition of Lan Xang, where the Lao monarchy exercises its authority and receives foreign embassies.

advances.name: Photisarath's Reforms
advances.text: King Photisarath's declaration of Theravada Buddhism as the state religion in 1527, unifying the spiritual life of the kingdom.

advances.name: Deer Skin Trade
advances.text: The export of deer skins, which were in high demand in China and Japan, funneled through Ayutthayan trade posts to reach distant markets.

advances.name: Firearms Adoption
advances.text: The adoption of matchlock firearms through contact with European and Asian traders during the golden age of Sourigna Vongsa.

advances.name: Golden Age of Lan Xang
advances.text: The fifty-seven-year reign of Sourigna Vongsa, a period of unprecedented peace, prosperity, and cultural flowering.

event.title: The Golden Age of Sourigna Vongsa
event.text:
For fifty-seven years, King Sourigna Vongsa has ruled Lan Xang with a steady hand. Where his predecessors faced invasion and civil war, Vongsa has achieved something remarkable, lasting peace with both Siam and Vietnam through patient diplomacy and firm borders.

In 1641, a Dutch trading expedition under Gerrit van Wuysthoff navigated the Mekong from Cambodia to Vientiane, marveling at the wealth they found. Lan Xang exports silk, gold, ivory, deer skins, cardamom, and benzoin resin to markets as distant as China and Japan.

But Vongsa is also known as a stern lawgiver. When his own son was found guilty of adultery, the king had him executed rather than grant exception. His laws are harsh but they are applied to all equally: noble and peasant alike.

How shall we build upon this golden age?

options.text: The law must be iron: no exceptions.

modifiers.name: The Strict Law
modifiers.text: Following Sourigna Vongsa's example, the kingdom enforces its laws with unwavering precision. Even the king's own family is not above justice, order flows from consistent authority.

options.text: Open our doors wider to the world.

modifiers.name: The Open Borders
modifiers.text: The golden age of Sourigna Vongsa proves that prosperity comes from welcoming the world. Dutch merchants, Chinese traders, and artisans from across the region bring their skills and their gold to the court at Vientiane.

advances.name: European Contact
advances.text: The arrival of Dutch VOC traders in 1641 opened Lan Xang to European commerce and knowledge for the first time.

advances.name: Law Code of Sourigna Vongsa
advances.text: The strict but egalitarian legal system established by Sourigna Vongsa, applied without exception to noble and commoner alike.

advances.name: Manuscript Tradition
advances.text: The Buddhist tradition of copying sacred texts onto palm-leaf manuscripts, preserving and spreading Pali learning throughout the kingdom.

advances.name: Lao Cultural Resilience
advances.text: The persistence of Lao cultural identity through centuries of division and foreign pressure, bound together by shared language, faith, and tradition.

advances.name: Mekong Mastery
advances.text: The full exploitation of the Mekong River system for transportation, trade, and resource extraction.

advances.name: Sangha Unity
advances.text: The Buddhist monastic network that binds the Lao people together across political boundaries, providing education, social cohesion, and spiritual continuity.

advances.name: Reunification Aspiration
advances.text: The enduring dream of restoring the borders of Fa Ngum's kingdom, uniting all Lao-speaking peoples under a single crown once more.

destiny.name: Destiny of Lan Xang
destiny.text: The kingdom stands restored. Now its destiny must be forged, through the thunder of elephants or the light of dharma.

event.title: The Restored Kingdom
event.text:
The ancient borders of Lan Xang are once more united under a single crown. From the highlands where the Mekong springs to the broad Khorat Plateau, the Land of a Million Elephants stands whole again.

But restoration is only the beginning. The great powers of Southeast Asia (Burma, Siam, Vietnam, and the Khmer) encircle our realm. Lan Xang has always lived in the shadow of greater neighbors, surviving through cunning, terrain, and the fearsome reputation of our war elephants.

The question now is whether we shall remain in that shadow, or step beyond it.

destiny.name: Khorat Subjugation
destiny.text: The kingdom's dominion is extended over the Shan highlands. The muang of Kengtung acknowledges Lan Xang's supremacy, by diplomacy or by force, and the war elephants of the crown are kept in three kraals.

conditions.text: Own Kengtung, or a subject owns it
An Elephant Kraal stands in at least 3 of our locations

event.title: The Shan Highlands Subdued
event.text:
The mountain fortress of Kengtung has submitted to the authority of Lan Xang. The Shan muang, long accustomed to playing the great powers against one another, have recognized that the Land of a Million Elephants is no longer content to remain within its traditional borders.

Our elephant corps moved through the highland passes with practiced ease, terrain that would have broken a lowland army was merely another day's march for our mahouts. The Shan saw the column approaching and knew that resistance meant destruction.

destiny.name: Mekong Hegemony
destiny.text: The great Khmer temples of Angkor, the Mekong crossroads at Stung Treng and Prey Nokor at the river's mouths fall under our control. The river belongs to Lan Xang from source to sea.

conditions.text: Own Angkor, or a subject owns it
Own Stœ̆ng Trêng, or a subject owns it
Own Prey Nokor, or a subject owns it

event.title: Masters of the Mekong
event.text:
The ancient temple complex of Angkor Wat, that wonder of the Khmer world, now flies the banner of Lan Xang. Our armies have swept down the Mekong, taking Stung Treng and establishing control over the great river's entire navigable length.

The Khmer, who once sheltered the exiled Fa Ngum and gave him armies to conquer these very lands, now find their positions reversed. The student has surpassed the teacher.

This hegemony can be consolidated through military dominance of the river, or through a tributary system that binds conquered peoples to our court.

options.text: Our river galleys shall patrol every reach.

modifiers.name: Mekong Dominance
modifiers.text: The Mekong is ours from source to sea, and our river galleys enforce our will upon every vessel that plies its waters.

options.text: Let the vanquished pay tribute and keep their customs.

modifiers.name: Vassal Tribute
modifiers.text: The conquered peoples pay tribute and serve in our levies, bound to Lan Xang by oath and obligation rather than direct occupation.

destiny.name: Lord of the White Elephants
destiny.text: Only a king who commands both Pegu and Ayutthaya, and whose elephants fill eight kraals, can claim dominion over all of mainland Southeast Asia. Let the white elephants bow to our throne.

conditions.text: Own Pegu, or a subject owns it
Own Ayodhya, or a subject owns it
An Elephant Kraal stands in at least 8 of our locations

event.title: Lord of the White Elephants
event.text:
Pegu and Ayutthaya, the capitals of Burma and Siam, kneel before the throne of Lan Xang. No Lao king has ever achieved what we have accomplished: dominion over the entire mainland of Southeast Asia, from the Irrawaddy to the Mekong delta.

The white elephants, rarest of all, have been gathered from every corner of the realm as symbols of universal sovereignty. In the court traditions of Southeast Asia, possession of white elephants is the ultimate mark of a righteous king whose merit shines across the world.

How shall we rule this vast domain?

options.text: As elephant lords: our war beasts enforce our will.

modifiers.name: Elephant Emperor
modifiers.text: The war elephants of Lan Xang are the finest in all of Asia, bred in royal compounds, armored in bronze, and commanded by the most skilled mahouts in the world.

options.text: As universal monarchs: our empire endures.

modifiers.name: Mekong Imperium
modifiers.text: A vast empire stretching across mainland Southeast Asia, held together by the Mekong River and the prestige of the Lao crown.

destiny.name: Heart of the Sangha
destiny.text: Let our kingdom become the beating heart of Theravada learning. With sound finances and the ivory trade flowing through our markets, we build wats in three of our towns, monasteries that will draw scholars from across the Buddhist world.

children.text: Elephants is produced in the market
Elephants is traded in the market

event.title: The Sangha Flourishes
event.text:
The monasteries of Lan Xang have become renowned throughout the Theravada world. Monks travel from as far as Ceylon and Burma to study at our wats, drawn by the quality of our Pali scholarship and the generous patronage of the crown.

The elephant trade, that most iconic commerce of our kingdom, fills the royal treasury, funding the construction of new temples and the copying of sacred manuscripts. Wats of the crown's founding now stand in three of our towns, and the merit of their building is counted in every village.

options.text: The dharma grows stronger every day.

destiny.name: The Mekong Silk Road
destiny.text: Silk, ivory, benzoin, deer skins: the products of our forests and looms must reach every market in Asia. Let Vientiane become the crossroads of the Mekong trade.

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

conditions.text: We own Vientiane and its development is at least 29

event.title: The Mekong Silk Road
event.text:
Vientiane has become the great crossroads of the Mekong basin. Silk from our looms, ivory from our forests, and benzoin incense from our highlands flow downriver to meet Chinese porcelain, Indian cloth, and European curiosities flowing upriver.

The Dutch merchant van Wuysthoff, upon visiting our capital, reported to his superiors that the wealth of Lan Xang rivaled any kingdom in the East. Our markets teem with goods from every corner of Asia.

Shall we press our advantage through mercantile expansion or through developing our domestic craft traditions?

options.text: Let our merchants range far along the Mekong.

modifiers.name: River Merchants
modifiers.text: The merchants of Vientiane range up and down the Mekong, their boats laden with silk and ivory, connecting the highland forests to the sea.

options.text: Let our artisans perfect their crafts at home.

modifiers.name: Craft Guilds
modifiers.text: The artisan guilds of Lan Xang have organized into powerful bodies, their silk weavers, lacquer workers, and ivory carvers producing goods that rival any in Asia.

destiny.name: Light of Theravada
destiny.text: The dharma shall radiate from our kingdom as light from a golden stupa. Let Muang Sua, the city of the Phra Bang, grow into a seat of learning with a library of its own that draws monks from every Buddhist land. With learning, prosperity, and faith, Lan Xang becomes the spiritual center of all Buddhist peoples.

conditions.text: We own Muang Sua and its development is at least 41
We own Muang Sua and it has a Library

event.title: Light of Theravada
event.text:
The great monasteries of Lan Xang have become the foremost centers of Theravada learning in all of Asia. Our palm-leaf manuscripts, copied with meticulous care by generations of monks, preserve the Pali canon in its purest form. Scholars from every Buddhist kingdom send their brightest pupils to study at our viharas.

A royal library now stands in Muang Sua beside the shrine of the Phra Bang, and its scribes copy the sacred scriptures without end, sending them as gifts to monasteries across the Buddhist world.

Lan Xang has become what Fa Ngum dreamed: not merely a kingdom, but a beacon of the dharma. The white parasol shelters all.

options.text: The dharma protects those who protect it.

modifiers.name: Shield of Dharma
modifiers.text: The sangha protects the kingdom as surely as any army. Our monks carry the dharma to every corner of the realm, binding the people together in faith.

options.text: Our stupas shall inspire the faithful forever.

modifiers.name: The Golden Stupa
modifiers.text: Our stupas, clad in gold leaf and rising above the jungle canopy, draw pilgrims and merchants from across the Buddhist world, filling our kingdom with devotion and prosperity.

units.name: War Elephant
units.text: The war elephants that gave Lan Xang its name. These armored behemoths serve as mobile fortresses on the battlefield, crushing enemy formations with sheer mass while their mahouts hurl javelins from above.

units.name: Elephant Corps
units.text: A formalized corps of war elephants trained under the reforms of Setthathirath. Each elephant carries a howdah with trained warriors, functioning as a combined-arms platform of devastating power.

units.name: Mekong River Guard
units.text: Infantry trained in the treacherous jungles and river crossings of the Mekong basin. They excel at ambush warfare and can move through terrain that would stop a conventional army.

units.name: Lao Matchlock Infantry
units.text: Infantry equipped with matchlock firearms acquired through European and Asian trade contacts during the golden age of Sourigna Vongsa.

units.name: Lao River Galley
units.text: Shallow-draft galleys designed for the Mekong River and its tributaries. Fast and maneuverable, they patrol the kingdom's waterways and protect merchant traffic.

buildings.name: Wat
buildings.text: A Buddhist temple complex that serves as the spiritual and educational center of the community. Monks teach reading and writing, preserve manuscripts, and provide counsel to all who seek it.

buildings.name: Silk Weaving House
buildings.text: A workshop dedicated to the ancient Lao art of silk weaving, producing textiles of extraordinary beauty and value using techniques passed down through generations.

buildings.name: Elephant Kraal
buildings.text: A royal compound for the capture, training, and holding of war elephants. The kraal is both a military facility and a symbol of royal power.

buildings.name: Mekong Trading Post
buildings.text: A riverside warehouse and dock where goods from the Lao highlands (silk, ivory, benzoin, and deer skins) are loaded onto boats for transport along the Mekong to distant markets.

buildings.name: Pha That Stupa
buildings.text: A grand Buddhist reliquary stupa, built in the tradition of Pha That Luang in Vientiane. Its golden surface draws pilgrims and artisans from across the Buddhist world.

buildings.name: Haw Kham
buildings.text: The royal palace of the Lao monarchy, from which the king administers justice and receives foreign embassies. Its ornate architecture reflects the wealth and sophistication of the court.

buildings.name: Rice Paddy
buildings.text: Paddy fields of glutinous rice, the foundation of Lao diet and communal life, watered by weirs the village keeps in common. Land with its weirs kept in good repair yields more rice.

where.text: The location's raw material is Rice

buildings.name: Forest Gathering Camp
buildings.text: A highland camp for harvesting benzoin resin, lac, and other valuable forest products from the dense woodlands of the Lao interior.

where.text: Incense is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Ivory Carvers' Workshop
buildings.text: A workshop where tusks from the royal herds and the upland tribute are carved into sword hilts, manuscript covers, and the paired tusks set beside a Buddha image. It is found where ivory or elephants reach the market.

children.text: Ivory is produced in the location's market
Elephants is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Ho Tai
buildings.text: The scripture library of a wat. Monks incise the Pali texts on dried palm leaves, blacken the cuts with soot, and bind the leaves between lacquered wooden covers.

buildings.name: Royal Elephant Compound
buildings.text: A grand royal complex for the breeding, training, and armoring of war elephants on an industrial scale, producing the finest battle elephants in all of Southeast Asia.

buildings.name: Great Vihara
buildings.text: A magnificent Buddhist learning hall and monastery complex, the foremost center of Pali scholarship in the Theravada world, drawing monks and pilgrims from across Asia.

list.name: Senabodi
list.text: The high council of senior ministers (maha-sena and thao phraya) through which the Cao paramount-king ruled Lan Xang. Codified under Samsenthai (r. 1373-1416), the Senabodi was a closed circle drawn from a handful of great court houses; its concentration of authority in aristocratic hands made the central government formidable so long as the council held together, but produced the factional rivalries that fractured the kingdom into Vientiane, Luang Prabang, and Champasak in 1707.

list.name: Mueang-Long Ritual Center
list.text: The sacred royal city as the ritual-political heart of the kingdom: Muang Sua under Fa Ngum, then Vieng Chan from 1560 under Setthathirath. The Phra Bang Buddha (gifted by the Khmer court c. 1359) and from 1565 the Phra Keo Emerald Buddha at Wat Pha Kaeo were the kingdom's palladia. The Bun Phra Wet annual cycle, the That Luang stupa festival, and the royal ploughing rite bound dynasty, sangha, and capital into a single ritual order whose collapse traced the kingdom's own.

list.name: Sangha-Raja Hierarchy
list.text: The Theravada Buddhist hierarchy formalised by Fa Ngum and his Khmer queen Keo Kaengkanya, with the royally appointed Sangha-Raja resident at Wat That Luang as head of the order. The wat-school network taught Pali, doctrine, and Lao tham script, producing the literate stratum of village headmen and scribes. Its expansion came at the cost of the older satsana phi spirit-cults, alienating the forest-dwelling Khmu and the upland peoples whose worship lay outside the sangha's reach.

list.name: Khoa-aphai Vassal Compact
list.text: The tributary compact by which the great vassal mueang of the Lan Xang sphere (Phuan at Xieng Khouang, the Sipsongchuthai twelve cantons, Houaphanh, the Khorat tributaries) rendered annual kham-kong tribute in silver, lacquer, and textiles to the Cao while keeping their hereditary chao-mueang and local courts. The compact extended royal reach without direct administration but structurally shared sovereignty with the periphery, a fragility that fractured under Burmese and Vietnamese pressure after 1560.

list.name: Kha-Lao Upland Tribute
list.text: The extractive system by which lowland Lao chao-mueang and Mekong-valley merchants drew annual tribute in forest goods (cardamom, benzoin, sticklac, eaglewood, deer-skins, elephant ivory) from the Khmu, Ksing-Mul, and other upland peoples collectively termed kha (servant). The tribute supplied the Mekong long-distance trade with Ayutthaya and Hue while entrenching the second-class legal status of the highland populations, the structural fault that repeatedly ignited upland revolts.
